chapters.title: Chapter 6: Backtesting Alternative Data Strategies Rigorously

lessons.title: Survivorship Bias and Coverage Gaps in Alternative Data

body.text: The previous lesson was about using the wrong list at the wrong time. This one is about a subtler problem: what if the failures were never in the list at all, no matter how carefully you handle dates?

children.text: Lesson 1's universe selection trap was a data engineering mistake, using today's index list retroactively, that a properly built point-in-time membership history fixes. Survivorship bias is different and can persist even after you fix that: it happens when the underlying data source itself never captured the companies that failed, delisted, or disappeared, so there is nothing to correctly date in the first place, only a gap where those failures should be.
Classic Survivorship Bias: The Failures You Never See

A backtest built only from companies that are still listed and healthy today systematically excludes every company that went through bankruptcy, liquidation, or forced delisting along the way, such as Reliance Communications following its insolvency proceedings. Those companies typically posted large, negative returns before disappearing from the market. Leave them out of a historical average, and the remaining 'survivors' make the past look considerably better than it actually was to anyone invested across the whole period.
Quantifying the Damage: A Weighted-Average Illustration

Suppose a strategy's backtest universe, built only from companies that are still listed today, shows an average annualized return of 15% across 50 companies. During the actual backtest period, 5 additional companies were part of the true, correctly point-in-time universe, but they failed and delisted along the way, each posting a return of roughly -80% before disappearing.

body.title: Calculate the True, Survivorship-Corrected Average Return
body.prompt: 50 surviving companies averaged a 15% return, and 5 additional companies that failed during the period each returned roughly -80% before delisting. Treating this as an equal-weighted average across all 55 companies that were genuinely part of the universe, what is the correctly blended average return, as a percentage, to one decimal place?
body.explanation: Blended average = (50 x 15% + 5 x -80%) / 55 = (750 - 400) / 55 = 350 / 55 = 6.36%, which rounds to 6.4%. Excluding just 5 failed companies out of 55, roughly 9% of the true universe, cut the reported average return by more than half, from a survivorship-biased 15% down to a true 6.4%. Survivorship bias does not need to affect many companies to badly distort a result, it needs the excluded ones to have failed badly, which is exactly what failure looks like.

children.text: Alt-Data-Specific Survivorship: When the Vendor's Panel Itself Forgets Losers

Chapter 4 flagged that some app analytics panels only track apps once they reach a certain download rank, and simply stop reporting an app once it falls out of that range, rather than reporting a visible decline toward zero. This means the raw alternative data feed itself, independent of any backtest methodology you apply on top of it, only ever shows companies doing reasonably well, because the ones that genuinely failed quietly vanish from the panel instead of leaving a trail of bad numbers behind them. No amount of correct knowledge-date handling fixes this, because the missing observations were never delivered by the vendor in the first place.
The Vendor Backfill Trap: Buying History That Was Never There

This connects directly back to Chapter 3's vendor sourcing process. A vendor advertising '5 years of history for today's top 50 companies' has told you the panel's current membership rule, not necessarily its historical one. If that backfill was reconstructed by looking at which companies are relevant today and pulling their history, rather than a true point-in-time record of who was relevant at each past date, it silently carries the same survivorship gap as any other backward-looking universe construction.

body.title: Reading a Vendor's Backfill Claim Carefully
body.scenario: A web traffic vendor's sales deck states: 'Our platform provides 5 years of historical traffic data for the current top 200 e-commerce and retail apps in India.' Your desk is evaluating this vendor as part of the Chapter 3 sourcing process for a signal that needs a genuinely survivorship-free backtest.
body.prompt: What specific question does this claim leave unanswered, and what would you ask the vendor before trusting the backfill for a rigorous backtest?
body.modelAnswer: The claim describes the panel's current membership rule, the top 200 apps today, without stating whether the 5 years of history reflects who was actually in the top 200 at each point during those 5 years, or whether it was reconstructed only for the apps that happen to be in today's top 200, silently excluding any app that was prominent 3 years ago but has since fallen out of the ranking or failed entirely. The specific question to ask is whether the historical panel is point-in-time, meaning it would have included an app that was top 200 in year one even if that app no longer qualifies today, or whether it is reconstructed backward from today's list. If the vendor cannot answer this clearly or confirms it is reconstructed from today's list, the backfill should be treated as carrying a real survivorship gap, and any backtest built on it needs to be flagged and interpreted with that limitation explicitly in mind.

body.title: Practical mitigations when a fully survivorship-free feed isn't available

children.text: Cross-check the alt data vendor's coverage against an independent, genuinely point-in-time universe list, such as the index membership history from the previous lesson, and explicitly flag any company that should have appeared in the alt data feed at some point but never did. Where a clean fix isn't available, assume the backtest carries an optimistic bias and size any resulting strategy more conservatively than the raw numbers alone would suggest, rather than treating the reported IC or return as the honest, final answer.

body.text: Survivorship bias is dangerous precisely because it doesn't look like a bug. Every individual data point in a survivorship-biased backtest can be completely accurate, correctly dated, correctly sourced, and the overall result can still be badly wrong, simply because of who was quietly left out.

The figures and vendor scenario in this lesson are illustrative teaching examples, not results from any real backtest or claims about any real vendor. Nothing here is a recommendation to trade any security.

points: Survivorship bias is distinct from the universe selection trap in the previous lesson: it happens when failed or delisted companies are missing from the source data itself, not just misdated
A backtest built only from companies still listed today, such as one that excludes Reliance Communications-style delisted names, systematically overstates historical performance

In this lesson's illustration, excluding just 5 out of 55 genuinely eligible companies, the ones that failed with roughly -80% returns, inflated the reported average return from a true 6.4% to a survivorship-biased 15%
Some alt data vendor panels drop coverage of a company once it falls out of a ranking threshold, rather than reporting its decline, silently building survivorship bias into the raw feed itself

A vendor's historical backfill claim should be checked for whether it is genuinely point-in-time or reconstructed backward from today's list of relevant entities, exactly the question raised during Chapter 3's vendor sourcing process

When a fully survivorship-free feed isn't available, cross-check against an independent point-in-time universe and size any resulting strategy conservatively rather than trusting the raw backtest numbers at face value
